es.example: Esos dos son uña y mugre desde la primaria.
es.exampleTranslation: Those two have been inseparable since elementary school.
es.regionNote: Mexican Spanish (also attested in the Andes, Honduras, and Panama per Oxford Languages). The Castilian equivalent is uña y carne, now this entry's alternative rather than its anchor. The folk logic differs slightly from the Castilian version: uña y carne reads nail and flesh as one body; uña y mugre reads the grime that always collects under the nail and can never quite be scrubbed out — same conclusion, earthier reasoning.

it.text: Essere come il cacio sui maccheroni
it.literal: to be like the cheese on the macaroni
it.meaning: To be a perfect fit; two things that complete each other.
it.example: Luca e Sara sono come il cacio sui maccheroni nei progetti: lei si occupa della parte burocratica e lui della parte più tecnica.
it.exampleTranslation: Luca and Sara are a perfect fit on projects: she handles the paperwork and he takes the technical side.

bridge.note: Spanish fuses; Italian combines. Uña y mugre is one body by accident of grime — the dirt that collects under the nail and never quite scrubs out, inseparable not by design but by habit. Il cacio sui maccheroni is two distinct things whose meeting is ideal. One says you cannot pull them apart; the other says they were made to go together.

interference.es_to_it: Calling lifelong friends 'come il cacio sui maccheroni' tells an Italian they complement each other well, not that they are inseparable.
interference.it_to_es: Uña y mugre overshoots a complementary working pair — a Spanish listener hears deep personal intimacy, not a good division of labour.
